title: Designing Highly Available Architecture
overview: This topic is about keeping a system usable: how availability is defined and calculated, why systems go down, and which tactics, redundancy schemes and reference architectures reduce downtime. It is the quantitative and tactical core of the course's availability theme, where you move from the numbers (series/parallel availability, MTBF/MTTR, nines) to design choices such as circuit breakers, bulkheads, active/active clusters, RAID, backups and multi-AZ deployments. For the exam, expect to compute availability for a set of components, explain a failure cause, and justify a redundancy or tactic choice against cost.
big_ideas: **Availability = (AST - DT) / AST.** For average uptime T_up and recovery time T_down, A = T_up / (T_up + T_down). State whether a question’s MTBF means uptime or the whole failure-to-failure cycle.

For **independent** components, series availability multiplies required components; parallel availability is one minus the product of failure probabilities. Parallel modelling assumes any survivor can provide the required service.
**Yearly downtime:** 99.9% = 8.76 hours; 99.99% = 52.56 minutes; 99.999% = 5.256 minutes; 99.9999% = 31.536 seconds (365-day year). Each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold.

Focus on **unplanned downtime** (failures); planned downtime (deployments) is reduced by continuous delivery. Every redundancy decision is a cost trade-off, so classify components as critical or non-critical first.
In distributed systems everything can fail and failures **cascade**: chain reactions, slow responses, retry storms, unbounded fan-in and dogpiles on restart.

Tactics fall into **detect, recover (prepare/repair, reintroduce), prevent**, plus analysis (static fault trees, dynamic chaos engineering). Key stability patterns: timeout/retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, backpressure, decoupling via queues.
Use hardware, server, data and network redundancy to remove single points of failure; use backups for recovery. Active/active can share load, but surviving nodes still need capacity after a failure.
Patterns climb from basic web app to load balanced, hot standby, clustered HA and wide-area load balancing; modern platforms (Kubernetes ReplicaSets, multi-AZ AWS) automate the same ideas.

sections.title: Availability, reliability and fault tolerance
sections.summary: Three related but different properties, the AST/DT availability formula, and the MTTR/MTTF/MTBF timing metrics.

items: **Availability**: readiness for use (the probability the system works as required)
**Reliability**: probability of performing its function **without failure** for a specified period under stated conditions
**Fault tolerance**: ability to keep **normal service** going even though a fault has occurred
**AST** = Agreed Service Time in hours for a timeframe (e.g. a month)
**DT** = downtime in that timeframe
**Example**: agreed to run all of a 720-hour month, down for 0.72 hours → (720 - 0.72)/720 = **99.9%** available
notes.foot: **Key message**: availability depends on failures and downtime.

items: The lecture's **61,320-hour** figure is an arithmetic error
**Convert consistently**
**MTTF** → average uptime before failure
**MTTR** → average recovery duration
**MTBF** → the lecture's timeline calls the entire failure-to-failure cycle MTBF, but its later formula uses MTBF as uptime
To avoid mixing conventions, write **A = uptime / (uptime + recovery)**, then map the given values

terms.def: Probability/readiness that the system works as required when needed.
Probability of failure-free operation for a specified period under stated conditions.
Normal service continues even though a fault has occurred.
Agreed Service Time and Down Time (hours) in the measured period.
Mean time to recover / to failure / between failures.

check.q: System A fails twice a year for 4 hours each time. System B fails every day for 3 seconds. Which is more available, which is more reliable, and which would you rather run a payment service on?

items: **B is more available**: about **18 minutes** down per year (**99.997%**) against A's **8 hours** (**99.91%**)
**A is more reliable**: it runs much longer **between failures**
**For payments**: B's daily failures could break **transactions in progress** → choose by which failure the service tolerates
a.foot: **High availability does not imply high reliability.**

check.q: A service is agreed to run 7 am to 7 pm on 22 working days a month. This month it was down for 2 hours at 3 am and 1 hour at noon. What is its availability?

items: Only the **noon outage** falls inside the agreed service time → **DT = 1 hour**
a.foot: The **3 am outage** does not count against this measure, which is why the **agreed service time** must be stated with any availability figure.

check.q: A service has MTTF of 999 hours and MTTR of 1 hour. You can either halve how often it fails or halve its recovery time. Which raises availability more?

items: **Halve failures**: 1998 / 1999 about **99.95%**
**Halve recovery**: 999 / 999.5 about **99.95%**
Up from **99.9%**, because each halves the **share of time spent recovering**
a.foot: Choose by **cost and side effects**: fewer failures also improves **reliability**, while faster recovery (**monitoring, automated failover**) is often cheaper to achieve.

steps.label: System up
steps.detail: The system is available. The time from becoming available until the next failure is the MTTF.

steps.label: Failure: system down
steps.detail: A fault stops service. Downtime now accumulates until recovery completes.

steps.label: Recovery complete
steps.detail: MTTR is the time to recover, including repair, from the failure back to a working system.

steps.label: Next failure
steps.detail: The failure-to-failure interval includes both recovery and uptime. The lecture labels this interval MTBF; its later formula uses a different MTBF convention, so define your terms before substituting.

sections.title: Availability calculations: nines, series and parallel
sections.summary: The exam-critical arithmetic: MTBF/MTTR formula, downtime per year, and combining components in series and parallel.

items: **A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)**
Lecture writes **A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)**, treating MTBF as average uptime
e.g. **999 hours up + 1 hour recovery** → 99.9%
If MTBF means the **full cycle** → **A = (MTBF - MTTR) / MTBF**
**Do not add recovery twice**

notes.foot: These correct rounding in the lecture table.

items: **Assumes** independent component states and that every component is required
e.g. two 99% components → **98.01%**
Result is **no greater than the weakest component**; equality is possible if the other components are perfect
**A = 1 - product(1 - Ai)**
For **independent replicas** when any one can meet the service requirement
e.g. two 99% replicas → **99.99%**
**Collapse each 99% redundant pair** → 99.99%

sub: PC, internet, shared filesystem and LDAP as required 99% components

items: This independent-component model **misses 95%**
**Improve** required unreplicated links; check whether every dependency is actually on the **service path**
**30-day, 24-hour service month** → 43,200 minutes
**Meets 99.9%**, but not 99.99%
A fraction such as **"3.5 nines"** is not a substitute for the actual result
**Loosely couple** critical services from non-critical ones
**Fault tolerance** → can preserve normal service
**Graceful degradation** → keeps an agreed reduced service
**Decide which outcomes count as available** for the requirement being measured

terms.def: Availability expressed as the count of 9s (99.9% = three nines).
For independent required components, multiply availability fractions; the result cannot exceed the weakest.
For independent replicas where any one suffices, one minus the product of their failure probabilities.
Loosely couple critical components from non-critical ones.
Reduced but working service after an error instead of total outage.

check.q: A chain has a CDN at 99.99%, a web server pair at 99.99%, a single application server at 99% and a database pair at 99.99%. The budget covers one improvement: upgrade the CDN to 99.999%, or add a second application server. Which?

items: **Second application server**: that tier → **99.99%**, chain about **99.96%**
**CDN upgrade**: only about **98.98%**
**In series the weakest component dominates**
a.foot: **Assumes** independent failures and enough **capacity in the surviving server**.

check.q: A teammate says two 99% servers in parallel give 99.99%, so the service now meets four nines. What must be true for that claim to hold?

items: **Independent failures**
**Failover must work and be fast**
**Either server can carry the full load alone**
**Rest of the request path** must also reach four nines, because everything **in series multiplies**
a.foot: **Shared power, storage or a common software bug** break the independence assumption and make 99.99% optimistic.

check.q: Two replicas share one power supply. Can you apply the independent parallel formula to the whole service?
check.a: Not without modelling the common dependency. Both replicas can fail together when power fails; put the required power supply in series with the replica group, or remove that shared failure domain.

check.q: An SLA promises 99.99% availability per year, and planned downtime counts. A database upgrade needs 2 hours offline. Can you do it without breaching the SLA?

items: **99.99% allows** (1 - 0.9999) x 525,600 = **52.56 minutes** of downtime a year → **2 hours** alone exceeds it
**Option 1**: upgrade without downtime (a **rolling upgrade** across redundant nodes)
**Option 2**: agree a **maintenance window** outside the **agreed service time**
a.foot: At **99.9%** (**8.76 hours** a year), the 2-hour upgrade would fit.

visuals.title: Series vs parallel availability
rows: No greater than the weakest required component
No less than the best replica
visuals.caption: Assumes independent states. The parallel case also assumes sufficient survivor capacity and effective failover.

sections.title: Improving availability: downtime causes and the architect's response
sections.summary: The approach to reducing downtime, planned vs unplanned downtime, the common causes at application, server and cloud level, and what an architect does about each.

notes.lead: There are **no fixed rules**, so follow **best practice** and get the most from **minimum resources**.
items: **Chart** the systems and IT resources
**Gather past downtime statistics** and compute availability
**Identify causes** (general and organisation-specific)
**Classify causes** as controllable or not
**Classify functions** as critical or non-critical
**Derive** infrastructure and architecture plans
**Weigh alternatives to optimise cost** (an essential trade-off)
**Planned** → mostly caused by **deployment**; attacked by **continuous delivery/deployment**
**Unplanned** → caused by **system failure**; the focus of this topic
heterogeneous environments
multiple single points of failure
multiple application interfaces
inadequate monitoring
resource bottlenecks
team silos
job failures
network issues
password expiry/locked accounts
employee attrition
**SOA/integration best practice and EA standardisation** → control variety
**Hardware, data, server and network redundancy** and **backups**
**Manual plus automated monitoring**
**Criticality analysis** with redundancy for critical sets
**People-related causes** are non-technical → need a **human-relations approach**

sub: training plans and audits for crucial functions
secure infrastructure (firewalls, DMZ, protection against DoS and malware)
load shedding with a threshold that balks further calls

items: **Noisy neighbour** → rate limits per user or IP
**Retry spikes** → a retry-control policy, since rejections cause retries
**Bad dependency** → load testing to find critical components
**Scaling boundaries** → sharding and clustering
**Uneven sharding** → split hot shards
**Pets** (hand-managed components) → train, automate
**Bad deployment** → phased rollout, systematic rollback
**Monitoring gaps** → monitor user experience
**Failure domains** → geographic redundancy and off-site backups

terms.def: Scheduled outage, usually for deployment; reduced by continuous delivery.
Outage caused by system failure.
Refusing calls above a defined threshold load to avoid a crash.
A greedy client or tenant consuming shared capacity; limit calls per user or IP.
A component whose failure takes the whole service down.

check.q: Leadership wants every system in the company engineered for 99.99% availability. Critique the directive.

items: **Cost**: each extra nine and each redundant component costs more → apply it **by criticality**
**Classify** functions as **critical or non-critical**
**Critical** → redundancy and the higher target; **accept lower targets** elsewhere
a.foot: The architect's job is to meet the **required availability at acceptable cost**, not to maximise it everywhere.

check.q: After load shedding is enabled at 80% CPU, incoming traffic to a service doubles within a minute. What is happening, and what is the fix?

a.lead: **Retry spikes**: rejected clients retry immediately, adding load to an already overloaded service.
items: **Retry policy**: limits and **backoff** on clients, alongside the **shedding threshold**
**Per-user rate limits** for greedy clients
a.foot: **Shedding without retry control** can make overload worse.

check.q: Last year's 14 hours of downtime came mostly from the monthly release process. What kind of downtime is this, and what would you change?

items: **Release windows → planned downtime** → reduced by **continuous delivery and deployment**
**Failed releases → unplanned downtime** → reduced by **phased rollouts** and **systematic rollback**
a.foot: Changing the **release process** likely cuts more downtime than adding **hardware redundancy**, which does not fix bad deployments.

check.q: One API client's nightly batch job floods a shared service and slows everyone else down. Which cloud-level cause is this, and how would you fix it?

items: **Rate limits per user or API key** (or per IP address)
**Sized** so normal clients are unaffected
a.foot: **Cost**: the batch client must spread its load or negotiate a **higher quota**.

sections.title: Failure sources in distributed systems
sections.summary: Why distributed systems fail in chains: every component and connection can fail, and defects propagate through cascades, heavy users, fan-in and restarts.

items: **Hardware, network and software**
In a distributed system **every component and every connection** can fail
A **crack in one component** can propagate to others
Instances behind a **load balancer** run **identical logic**
A bug such as a **memory leak** triggered by a specific operation crashes the instance that handles most of those operations first
The **survivors take more load** and fail faster
The **whole pool collapses**
**Upstream services must handle errors** from providers
**Slow responses** propagate trouble upward
**Speculative retries** make it worse
**Watch resource pools** (threads, connections) that fill while waiting on a slow dependency
**Heavy operations** → a special user such as a **celebrity** whose tweet fans out to many followers
**Scaling effect and unbounded capacity**: a service with **many fan-ins** is hit hard when an upstream service scales out
e.g. a **front end** of 20 hosts, 75 instances, 3,000 threads calling a **back end** of 6 hosts, 6 instances, 450 threads
**Dogpile** → after a restart, all services warm their in-memory caches by hitting the database at once

terms.def: One component's failure or slowness spreads to its callers and peers.
Survivors fail faster as a crashed instance's load shifts onto them.
Simultaneous cache warm-up hits on the database after a restart.
Many upstream services calling one common service.

check.q: Behind a load balancer, instance 1 crashes, then instance 2 crashes 20 minutes later, then the rest go within 10 minutes. What is the likely cause, and how would you confirm it?

items: **Same logic on all instances** → a bug such as a **memory leak** triggered by a particular operation kills the **busiest instance first**
**Survivors take its load** → fail faster
**Confirm**: check **memory growth** and the **request mix** on each instance before it crashed
a.foot: **Adding instances only delays the collapse**; fix or isolate the triggering operation.

check.q: For a marketing campaign the front end scales from 6 to 75 instances (3,000 threads), while the back end stays at 6 instances with 450 threads. What fails first, and what would you change?

items: **Many fan-ins, bounded capacity**: far more concurrent calls than its **450 threads** can serve
→ requests **queue**, **time out** and trigger **retries**
**Fix**: scale the back end **in step**, or cap calls with **backpressure** or **rate limits**
**Load-test** with the scaled-out front end

check.q: After a full restart, the database hits 100% CPU and the system takes 40 minutes to recover, although normal load is 30% CPU. Diagnose it and suggest a fix.

items: **Cause**: every service warms its **in-memory cache** from the database at the same moment, just as the database is recovering
**Fix**: bring services back **gradually**, not all at once
**Limit the rate of cache-fill queries** so the database is not swamped

check.q: A user with 30 million followers posts, and the notification service falls an hour behind. Which failure source is this, and what would you consider?

a.lead: **A heavy operation from a special user**: one action fans out to millions of deliveries.
items: **Handle such accounts differently**: e.g. **fetch their posts when followers read** rather than pushing to every follower
**Isolate their processing** so it cannot starve normal users

visuals.title: How a slow dependency spreads failure

steps.label: Dependency slows
steps.detail: A fault or overload in a downstream service increases how long callers wait.

steps.label: Pools fill
steps.detail: Waiting requests occupy finite upstream resources, leaving fewer slots for new work.

steps.label: Retries multiply load
steps.detail: Unbounded retries add demand while the dependency is already struggling.

steps.label: Callers fail
steps.detail: Timeouts and bounded retries limit waiting; circuit breakers and bulkheads contain the spread.

sections.title: Availability tactics and stability patterns
sections.summary: The tactic taxonomy (analysis, detection, recovery, prevention) and the practical stability patterns: circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, backpressure, decoupling and chaos engineering.

items: **Cut set**: a combination of basic events that causes the top failure
**Minimal** cut set: removing any event stops it causing that failure
Minimal need not mean the **smallest set** in the whole tree
**Singleton cut set** → identifies a single failure cause to address
**Ping/echo**
**Heartbeat** and **monitor**
**Exception tracking/detection**
**Timestamps**
**Sanity and condition checks**
**Voting** and **self-test**
**Remove suspect components** from service
**Transactions** and **process monitors**
**Prevent exceptions** through handling
**Expand the conditions** the system can handle (the lecture's **"increase competence sets"**)
**Closed** → permits calls
**Repeated failures trip it open** → fail fast
**After a delay, half-open** → permits trial calls; back to **closed on success**, **open on failure**
notes.foot: Choose an agreed **fallback** (cached value, generic response or explicit error), **expose state** to operators and **log transitions**. **Timeouts** bound waiting; **retries must be limited**.

items: **Steady state**: databases, in-memory caches and logs accumulate over time → have a strategy and implementation to **purge** them

sub: redundant copies of services, middleware and databases

items: Bulkheads **segregate critical components**, e.g. giving component C **two separate pools** so one pool's failure is contained
**Load shedding** → rejects or throttles excess requests
**Handshake** → checks whether a downstream instance can accept work
**Backpressure** → makes upstream producers slow down
**Circuit breaker** → can stop calls to a failed dependency, but does not itself make every producer reduce its rate
**Queues** → decouple timing, but still need capacity limits and failure handling
**Prepare** tracing and monitoring
**State a resilience hypothesis**
**Inject a fault**
**Analyse** targeted cases
**Automate and repeat**
notes.foot: Lecture example: **Netflix's Simian Army**. A meaningful experiment measures the **agreed service outcome**.

terms.def: A failure-causing combination of basic events with no removable event; it need not have globally minimum size.
Wrapper that fails fast when a dependency keeps failing (closed, open, half-open).
Partition that contains a failure so it cannot spread to other parts.
Moving overload pressure upstream instead of absorbing it downstream.
Controlled fault experiments that test resilience hypotheses using observed system behaviour.

check.q: A product page calls a recommendations service that sometimes hangs for 30 s. Design the protection: timeout, circuit-breaker behaviour and fallback.

items: **Timeout**: short, well below the page's response target, with **at most one retry**
**Fallback**: a generic list such as **best-sellers**
**Log state changes** for operators
a.foot: **Trade-off**: customers see less personalised pages while the breaker is open.

check.q: Payments and report generation share one database connection pool of 50. A slow report query exhausts the pool, and payments fail. What would you change?

items: **Separate connection pools** (or separate instances) for payments and reports
→ a report **cannot exhaust** the resources payments need
a.foot: **Cost**: less efficient sharing; one pool may sit idle while the other waits.

check.q: A fault tree for 'checkout unavailable' has minimal cut sets {DNS failure}, {primary database fails AND replica fails} and {payment gateway down}. Where do you focus first?

a.lead: **Focus on the singletons: DNS and the payment gateway.**
items: **Single-element cut sets**: each alone takes checkout down
**DNS** → add redundant DNS
**Payment gateway** → a second gateway, or a **degraded mode** such as holding orders for later payment
**Database** needs **two failures together** → already protected
a.foot: Provided the primary and replica really **fail independently**.

check.q: A team wants to start chaos engineering by randomly killing production database nodes next week. Critique the plan.

items: **Prerequisites**: **tracing and monitoring** that show the agreed service outcome
**State a hypothesis** ('losing one replica does not raise checkout errors')
**Inject a targeted, contained fault**
**Analyse** the result
**Only then automate and repeat**
a.foot: **Random destruction** without monitoring and a hypothesis teaches nothing and risks **real outages**.

visuals.title: Circuit breaker states

steps.label: CLOSED
steps.detail: Normal operation: the protected call goes through and failures are counted.

steps.label: OPEN
steps.detail: After failures exceed the threshold the breaker trips. Calls are not attempted; return a cached value, a generic answer or a different exception.

steps.label: HALF OPEN
steps.detail: After a certain period a trial call is allowed. If it succeeds the breaker resets to closed; if it fails it trips back to open.

visuals.caption: After half-open, success returns to closed; failure returns to open. Agree fallbacks and log every transition.

sections.title: Redundancy: hardware, server, software and data
sections.summary: Eliminating single points of failure with hardware, server (active/passive, active/active), software clustering and data redundancy including RAID levels.

notes.lead: Avoiding a single point of failure:
items: **Hardware redundancy**
**Data redundancy**
**Server redundancy**
**Network redundancy**
**Backup strategies**
**Redundant power** → hot-swap a failed supply without downtime
**Redundant cooling** → a fan failure can kill temperature-sensitive processor or memory
**Multiple processors** → also load balancing and scalability
**Memory** → hard errors are catastrophic failures; soft errors are random bit flips
**Network adapters** → in failover pairs
**RAID adapters** → as a failover pair
**Replicates compute, applications and configuration** to cover hardware or OS failures
**Cold spare** → needs startup
**Standby** → already prepared
**Cluster** → presents cooperating computers as a service
**Failover** → transfers service after failure; **failback** → returns it later
A **backup server** holding files does not by itself provide live compute failover
**Active/passive** → keeps a standby, detects failure with **heartbeats** and activates the replacement
**Active/active** → shares work across live instances
In both, plan **state handling**, **traffic switching** and **enough capacity after a loss**
A **floating IP** can move the endpoint but does not transfer application state
**RAID, SAN redundancy and duplicate data centres** → cover different failure domains
**Backups** → support recovery

sub: **3 and 4** → dedicated parity (lecture labels them bit- and block-interleaved)

items: **RAID 0** → 12 TB, no failure tolerance
**RAID 10** → 6 TB, survives any one failure and some two-failure combinations; loses data if **both members of the same mirror** fail
**RAID 5** → 9 TB, any one failure
**RAID 6** → 6 TB, any two failures
notes.foot: **Performance** depends on workload, controller and rebuild activity, not just the RAID number.

terms.def: Replacing a failed component (e.g. power supply) without shutting the system down.
Automatic switch to the backup on failure / the later return to the primary.
All nodes serve traffic, sharing the load behind a load balancer.
An address that can be moved between nodes to switch to a standby quickly.
Redundant Array of Independent Disks: striping, mirroring and parity for speed and fault tolerance.

check.q: A booking service keeps user sessions in local memory and must survive one server failure. Active/passive or active/active?

a.lead: **Active/active, if you can externalise the sessions** → more capacity.
items: **Active/active**: spreads load across live servers; survives one loss **only if sessions move** out of local memory into a **shared store**
**Active/passive**: simpler, but sessions are **lost at failover** unless replicated, and the **standby sits idle**
**Floating IP** (both): moves the **address, not the state**

check.q: You have four 3 TB disks, must survive any two disk failures, and need at least 6 TB usable. Which RAID level, and why not RAID 10?

items: **RAID 6**: two disks' worth of **parity** → **6 TB usable**, survives **any two failures**
**Not RAID 10**: also 6 TB but guarantees only **one failure**; two failures in the **same mirror** lose data
a.foot: **Cost**: RAID 6 pays with **parity overhead on writes**.

check.q: Two disks fail in a four-disk RAID 10 array. Is the data necessarily lost?
check.a: It depends on placement. One failure in each mirror leaves a working copy; both failures in the same mirror lose that stripe's copies. A failure count alone is insufficient.

check.q: A team says: 'We have a backup server with nightly copies of all files, so we have server redundancy.' Do you agree?

items: **Backup server supports recovery**, not **live compute failover**
**If the main server fails** → service down until a **restore and rebuild** finish
→ **long recovery time**, up to **a day of changes lost**
**Server redundancy** needs a **prepared standby** or **active peers with current state**

visuals.title: Four 3 TB disks: capacity versus protection
rows: Any one; two only in different mirrors
visuals.caption: RAID 1 row uses two disks; other rows use four. RAID handles disk failures, not accidental deletion or whole-site loss.

sections.title: Backup strategies: full, differential, incremental
sections.summary: Three backup types and their trade-off between backup effort and restore effort.

items: **Copies all files every time**
**Restore is easy** from a single set
Takes the **longest** and uses the **most disk, tape or network space**
**Copies files changed or new since the last full backup**
**Faster and smaller** than full
**Restore needs** the last full + the latest differential → restoring everything or locating one file is slower
**Example**: Monday full; Tuesday and Wednesday each back up everything changed since Monday's full, so Wednesday's set includes Tuesday's changes too
**Copies changes since the last backup** in the chain
Start with a **full base**, then take only new changes each time
**Restore requires** the base + every needed incremental, **in order**
Chain is **more complex** than a full-plus-latest-differential restore
**Full** → slow backup, fast restore
**Differential** → middle
**Incremental** → fast backup, slow restore
notes.foot: Backups protect against **data loss and disasters** but are a **recovery measure (they affect MTTR)**, not a substitute for live redundancy.

terms.def: Copies every file in the set each time.
Copies changes since the last full backup.
Copies changes since the previous backup in the chain; restoration needs a full base and the required increments.

check.q: A full backup runs Sunday night and incrementals run Monday to Friday nights. The disk fails on Saturday afternoon. What must you restore, and how would differential backups compare?

items: **Incrementals**: restore **Sunday's full**, then **all five incrementals** (Monday to Friday) **in order**; losing any one **breaks the chain**
**Differentials**: restore **Sunday's full** and only **Friday's differential** → simpler and faster
a.foot: Either way, **Saturday's changes** since Friday night are lost.

check.q: A full backup takes 6 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, and a full restore must finish within 4 hours. Which backup scheme fits?

items: **Nightly full doesn't fit**: 6 hours vs the 2-hour window
**Differential** is smaller than a full; a restore needs only **two sets**
**Check**: late-week differentials still fit the **2-hour window**, and full + differential restores within **4 hours**
a.foot: **Incrementals** fit the window best but make restores **slower and more fragile**.

check.q: A manager wants to remove the standby database because 'we already take hourly incremental backups'. Do you agree?

items: **Backups are a recovery measure** that affects **MTTR**, not live redundancy
**Restore** from a full plus many incrementals → **hours**, and loses up to **an hour of data**
**Standby** → takes over in **minutes**
a.foot: **Keep both**, or accept the much longer outage **explicitly**.

sections.title: Availability patterns for web applications
sections.summary: A progression of web-app topologies, each removing more single points of failure at higher cost.

items: **One web application server in the DMZ**
**Protocol firewall** → from the outside world
**Domain firewall** → to the internal network (directory/security services, database, shared file system)
**Every box is a single point of failure**
**Load balancer** in front of a **cluster** of web application servers
A failed server is **bypassed** and **capacity grows**
**With hot standby** → a standby load balancer or node is kept ready to take over, so the load balancer itself stops being a single point of failure
**Duplicates load balancers and web clusters**
**Check all required dependencies**, including storage, directory services, firewalls and networks
Redundancy drawn at the **web tier** does not establish redundancy for the **whole service**
**Global load balancer** spreads traffic across entire sites (**Site A and Site B**)
Each site has its own **firewalls, load balancer, web application servers, database and file system**
Protects against **whole-site (failure-domain) failure**
notes.foot: Each step up buys availability and **costs more**, so **match the pattern to the required nines**.

terms.def: Demilitarised zone: network segment between outside world and internal network holding public-facing servers.
A ready, running spare; takeover still requires detection, switching and any state recovery.
Distributing traffic across geographically separate sites.

check.q: A design has two load-balanced web servers behind one load balancer, with one database and one shared file system. Where are the single points of failure?

items: **The load balancer** → fix with a **hot standby**
**The database**
**The shared file system**
**Any single firewall or network link** on the path
a.foot: **Redundancy at the web tier** does not make the whole service redundant → check **every required dependency**.

check.q: The requirement is to survive the loss of an entire data centre and recover within 5 minutes. The current design is a high-availability topology at one site. What must change?

a.lead: **Add wide area load balancing** across a **second site**.
items: **Second site** has its own firewalls, load balancers, web servers, database and file system
**Data replicated** between the sites
→ removes the **single-site failure domain**
a.foot: **Cost**: roughly **double the infrastructure** plus the complexity of **cross-site data replication**.

check.q: An internal HR tool needs 99% availability, and a payments API needs 99.99%. Which availability patterns would you pick for each?

items: **HR tool (99%)**: a **basic or load-balanced web application** is likely enough; 99% allows about **3.65 days** of downtime a year
a.foot: Each step up costs more → **match the pattern to the required nines**.

steps.label: Basic web app
steps.detail: Single web application server between two firewalls; every component is a single point of failure.

steps.label: Load balanced
steps.detail: Several web application servers behind a load balancer; failed servers are bypassed.

steps.label: Hot standby
steps.detail: A ready spare removes the single load balancer or node as a single point of failure.

steps.label: High availability
steps.detail: Redundant balancers and clusters protect the front end. Inspect internal storage, directory, network and firewall dependencies before claiming end-to-end availability.

steps.label: Wide area load balancing
steps.detail: A global load balancer spreads traffic across two full sites, surviving a whole-site failure.

sections.title: Reference architectures: Kubernetes, databases and AWS
sections.summary: How Kubernetes self-heals, how database servers achieve redundancy across the active/passive and shared disk/shared nothing models, and the multi-AZ AWS reference.

items: **ReplicaSet** → replaces terminated pods to maintain the replica count
**Liveness probes** → can trigger container restart
Replacement **takes time** and needs **working capacity**
These **shorten recovery** but do not establish **data redundancy** or prevent a **shared-node failure**
**Database server process** → handles queries
**Storage** → data
**Oracle RAC** → active/active, shared disk
**SQL Server failover clustering** → active/passive, shared disk
**Database mirroring** → active/passive, separate storage
**MySQL primary/replica** → writes on one primary, reads can be served on replicas; its **"active/active" label does not mean multiple write leaders**
**Cassandra** → replicates across ring nodes with configurable replica counts
**Spread application instances across Availability Zones**
**Load balancer** directs traffic to healthy instances
**Replacing a host or remapping an address** restores reachability, not lost data
Lecture distinguishes **live storage replication within a zone** from **point-in-time snapshots**
**Cross-zone recovery** also requires an explicit data and restore plan
**Understand components and failure causes** to build the plan
**Key concepts** → availability, reliability, fault tolerance
**Key decisions** → redundancy, backup, patterns

terms.def: Kubernetes controller that keeps a set number of pod copies running.
Health check that lets Kubernetes restart an unhealthy container.
Database nodes share one storage; disk redundancy is handled by hardware.
Each node has its own storage; data is replicated between nodes.
An isolated location within a cloud region used to survive single-location failure.

check.q: A team says Kubernetes will make their single-instance database highly available because it restarts failed pods. Do you agree?

items: **Restarting or rescheduling the pod** → shortens recovery
But the **database is still down** while it restarts
A restart gives the data **no redundant copy**
**Node or storage failure** can still lose service or data
a.foot: Add **replication across nodes**, or a **managed redundant database**, and **test recovery**.

check.q: A two-node active/passive database cluster uses one shared storage array, and the array fails. What happens, and what alternative avoids it?

items: **Shared disk** delegates redundancy to the storage → the **array is a single point of failure**
**Shared-nothing**: each node owns its storage and data is **replicated** → avoids it
a.foot: **Cost**: managing **replication and promotion**.

check.q: A primary/replica database loses its primary at peak time. What happens to reads and writes, and what does recovery involve?

items: **Reads** can continue on the **replica**
**Writes stop** until a replica is **promoted** to primary, because only the primary accepts writes
**Promotion takes time**; writes **not yet replicated may be lost**
a.foot: **Read replicas** provide read capacity and redundancy, not **independent write leaders**.

check.q: Application instances are spread across two availability zones, but the database runs in one zone and is protected by periodic snapshots. That zone fails. What happens?

a.lead: **Compute survives, but the service loses its data tier.**
items: **Restoring from a snapshot** takes time and loses **every change since the snapshot**
**Spreading compute alone is not enough**
**Fix**: **replicate the database across zones**, or plan an explicit **data recovery** that meets the **recovery target**

visuals.title: Database redundancy models
rows: Redundant nodes for the process; disk redundancy delegated to hardware
SQL Server Always On failover clustering
Only one node uses the storage at a time
Lecture calls this active/active; write failover still needs promotion
Configurable replicas; virtual nodes rebalance automatically

exam_angles.q: A web system has an active/passive load balancer pair (99% each), two web servers in parallel (99% each), one application server (99%), an active/passive database pair (99% each) and one firewall (98%). The target is 99.9%. Calculate end-to-end availability, say whether it meets the target, and recommend improvements with their assumptions.

a.lead: **96.99%: misses 99.9%**; replicating the app server and firewall gives **99.92%**.
items: **In series**: 0.9999^3 x 0.99 x 0.98 = **96.99%** → misses **99.9%** badly because of the **single application server and firewall**
**Replicate both**: 0.9999^4 x (1 - 0.02^2) = **99.92%** → just meets the target
**Assumes**: **independent failures**, **working failover** and **enough capacity in the survivors**
a.foot: **Shared power, storage or a common software fault** would lower the real figure → **test failover** and check for **shared failure domains**.

exam_angles.q: A monthly SLA promises 99.95% over a 30-day, 24-hour service month. This month had a 15-minute unplanned outage and a 20-minute planned maintenance window. Does the service meet the SLA? What changes the answer, and what would you change in the design?

a.lead: **Passes if planned maintenance is excluded; fails if it counts.**
items: **Month** = **43,200 minutes**; **99.95%** allows **21.6 minutes** of downtime
**Outage alone**: 15 minutes (**99.965%**) → **passes**
**Planned maintenance counts**: total 35 minutes (**99.919%**) → **fails**
**What changes the answer**: whether the **agreed service time excludes the maintenance window**

sub: **Rolling or blue/green deployments** → maintenance needs no downtime
**Faster detection and failover** → shorter unplanned outages

exam_angles.q: Service A receives 100 requests/s and has 200 worker threads. Each request calls service B with a 30 s timeout. B slows from 50 ms to 10 s per call. Explain what happens to A, and design the containment.

sub: **Little's Law**: A needs 100 x 10 = **1,000** requests in flight but has **200 threads**
→ A stops responding and **its own callers fail**, made worse by **retries**
**Short timeout**: 1 s would keep about **100 requests** in flight
**Circuit breaker**: fails fast with a **fallback** once B is unhealthy
**Bulkhead**: calls to B use their own limited pool, so they cannot take every thread

items: **Validate**: inject latency into B in a **chaos experiment**

exam_angles.q: An e-commerce site needs 99.99% availability for checkout. The data tier is the weak point. Compare two database redundancy models and recommend one, stating what you would monitor.

a.lead: **Prefer shared-nothing replication across failure domains** for 99.99%.
items: **Active/passive with shared disk**: simple failover, but the **shared storage is a single point of failure** unless the array itself is redundant

**Shared-nothing replication** (a primary with replicas, or multi-node replication): each node has **its own storage** → avoids that, but needs **promotion rules** and risks **losing unreplicated writes** at failover

sub: **Automated, tested promotion** and **enough capacity in the survivors**
**Failover time** and **data loss** in failover tests

a.foot: **Calculate end-to-end availability** rather than trusting the topology label.

exam_angles.q: A database holds 2 TB. A full backup takes 5 hours, the nightly window is 2 hours, daily changes are about 50 GB, and the recovery-time target is 3 hours. Compare full, differential and incremental backup and recommend a scheme.

a.lead: **Weekly full + nightly differentials**, if day-six differentials fit the window.
items: **Nightly full**: **impossible** (5 hours against a 2-hour window)
**Weekly full + nightly incrementals**: copies only about **50 GB** a night, but a late-week restore needs the full plus **up to six incrementals in order** → **slowest and most fragile**
**Weekly full + nightly differentials**: grows to about **300 GB by day six**, which must still fit the window; restore needs only **the full plus one differential**
**Then test** whether a **2 TB full restore** can finish within **3 hours**
a.foot: If it cannot, **backups alone cannot meet the target** → you need a **standby replica**.

exam_angles.q: Choose a RAID level for an array of four 3 TB disks that must tolerate any two simultaneous disk failures, and state its cost against the alternatives.

items: **Tolerance**: guarantees **any two disk failures**, with at least **four disks**
**Capacity**: two disks' worth holds **parity** → four 3 TB disks provide **6 TB usable**
**Cost**: **parity updates add write overhead**; actual speed depends on workload and implementation

sub: **RAID 10**: same **6 TB** but guarantees only **one failure** (two only if they are in **different mirrors**)
